w: At 1,085 metres, Yr Wyddfa is the highest peak in Wales, its pyramidal summit and knife-edge aretes of Crib Goch and Y Lliwedd carved by volcanoes and glaciers. Six paths climb it, but most walk up from Llanberis - or ride the 1896 rack railway; 543,541 walkers reached the top in 2022 alone.
s: Wales's highest peak, climbed by rack railway since 1896
_facts: Six main paths to the summit, Llanberis most popular

w: Edward I raised this fortress in just four years, 1283-1287, at a ruinous cost, as the anchor of his new walled town. It withstood a Welsh siege in 1294-95, sheltered a fugitive Richard II in 1399, and held out for Charles I until 1646. UNESCO now ranks it among Europe's finest 13th-century military architecture.
s: Edward I's fortress that outlasted a king and a siege
_facts: Built 1283-1287 for Edward I, cost c.£15,000

w: Thomas Telford's 1826 span across the Menai Strait was one of the world's first major suspension bridges and only the second ever built to carry wheeled traffic. It linked Anglesey to the mainland for the first time without a ferry crossing. Grade I listed, it still carries live traffic today, nearly two centuries on.
s: Telford's 1826 bridge, one of the world's first
_facts: Second suspension bridge ever to carry vehicles
Grade I listed, still carries road traffic

w: Edward I's last and largest Welsh castle was never finished - work stalled when funds were diverted to his Scottish wars, and stopped for good around 1330. Welsh forces seized it in 1403 during Owain Glyndwr's rising. In 1592 the priest William Davies was imprisoned here before his execution in the yard the next year.
s: The unfinished last castle of Edward I's conquest
_facts: Building began 1295 under James of St George

w: Perched on a rocky knoll above the Irish Sea, Harlech fell to Owain Glyndwr in 1404 and became his residence and HQ for the rest of his uprising. Its seven-year Lancastrian defence in the Wars of the Roses inspired the song 'Men of Harlech.' It held out longest of any Civil War fortress, surrendering in 1647.
s: The castle behind the song 'Men of Harlech'
_facts: Last fortress to surrender in the Civil War, 1647

w: Robert Stephenson's tubular wrought-iron bridge, its foundation stone laid in 1846, closed the last rail gap between London and the Holyhead ferries to Dublin. The Admiralty insisted the spans sit high enough for a fully rigged warship to pass beneath - a demand that pushed Stephenson to pioneer tubular bridge design.
s: Stephenson's tubular bridge built to clear a warship
_facts: Built to Admiralty height requirement for warships

w: Wales's largest natural lake was already record-holder before Thomas Telford raised its level to feed the Llangollen Canal. The River Dee, rising on the slopes of Dduallt in Snowdonia, feeds its 3.7-mile length. A narrow-gauge steam line, the Bala Lake Railway, runs along the south-eastern shore on trackbed salvaged from the old Ruabon-Barmouth line, linking Bala to Llanuwchllyn.
s: Wales's largest lake, with its own narrow-gauge railway
_facts: Level raised by Thomas Telford for the Llangollen Canal
Bala Lake Railway runs along south-eastern shore

w: Llywelyn the Great built this round-towered keep - called the finest surviving example of its kind in Wales - to guard the Llanberis Pass and project his own power. When Edward I captured it in 1284, he stripped its timbers to help build his new castle at Caernarfon. By the 18th century it had become a magnet for painters chasing the Sublime and Picturesque; it's now a Cadw ruin above the pass.
s: Llywelyn the Great's round tower above Llanberis Pass
_facts: Built by Llywelyn the Great, early 13th century
Keep called finest surviving Welsh round tower
Captured by Edward I 1284, timbers reused at Caernarfon

w: Llywelyn ab Iorwerth, ruler of Gwynedd, raised this hill castle between 1210 and 1240 to guard a key east-west route, replacing an older tower, Tomen Castell, just downhill. Edward I seized it in 1283 during his conquest of Wales; by the 19th century it was a ruin, until Peter Drummond-Burrell rebuilt the keep in 1848-50. It's now a scheduled Cadw monument open to the public.
s: A Welsh prince's castle rebuilt by a Victorian baron
_facts: Begun by Llywelyn ab Iorwerth c.1210-1240
Superseded the older Tomen Castell tower

w: Two generations of Welsh princes built this headland fortress above Tremadog Bay - Llywelyn ap Iorwerth began it in the 1230s, his grandson Llywelyn ap Gruffudd extended it. Edward I captured it in 1283 and used it to imprison high-status captives, including Scottish prisoners of war. Rebels likely burned it during Owain Glyndwr's revolt in 1404; it was ruinous within decades.
s: A princes' castle turned royal prison on Tremadog Bay
_facts: Extended by grandson Llywelyn ap Gruffudd

w: One of the first road suspension bridges ever built anywhere, this Grade I-listed span once carried the main Chester-to-Bangor road straight past the walls of medieval Conwy. It's foot traffic only now, kept by the National Trust, its chains still holding a deck that predates almost every other road suspension bridge on earth.
s: One of the world's very first road suspension bridges
_facts: One of the world's first road suspension bridges
Now foot traffic only, kept by National Trust

w: The Aran range's highest summit is the only peak in Wales outside north Snowdonia to top 900 metres, and the county top of old Merionethshire. On its eastern flank sits Creiglyn Dyfi, a small glacial lake that is the source of the River Dyfi. Its sister peak, Aran Benllyn, rises just to the north at 885 metres, with Erw y Ddafad-ddu forming a middle summit between them.
s: Southern Wales's one 900-metre peak outside Snowdonia
_facts: Highest peak in the Aran range
Creiglyn Dyfi on its slopes is source of River Dyfi

w: The cathedral church of Saints Asaph and Cyndeyrn traces its foundation back 1,400 years, though the building standing today dates from the 13th century. It remains the seat of the Bishop of St Asaph in the Church in Wales - a small, ancient cathedral tucked into a modest Denbighshire town rather than a grand city.
s: A 1,400-year-old bishopric in a tiny cathedral town
_facts: Seat of the Bishop of St Asaph

w: This rocky, wooded knoll rising 76 metres above the Glaslyn valley carries the name 'Emrys's city' and the remains of an Iron Age hillfort - stone ramparts and a keep base still visible - overlooking Llyn Dinas. Some believe Llywelyn the Last built a castle here to guard the road up to Snowdon. Little else survives, but the site's name and setting have long drawn legend-hunters.
s: A wooded hillfort said to guard the road to Snowdon
_facts: Remains of an Iron Age hillfort and keep base
Linked in tradition to Llywelyn the Last

w: Wales's fourth-highest peak carries the name of Dafydd ap Gruffudd, younger brother of the last independent Prince of Wales, captured nearby in 1283 and executed at Shrewsbury. Its flat, boulder-strewn summit is reached along the ridge from Pen yr Ole Wen, with the crags of Ysgolion Duon dropping away to the north.
s: A Carneddau summit named for an executed Welsh prince
_facts: Crags of Ysgolion Duon lie to the north

w: This shallow ribbon lake, barely three metres at its deepest, sits between the Carneddau and Glyderau ranges and carries a great Arthurian legend. After the Battle of Camlann, Sir Bedivere is said to have cast Excalibur into its waters, caught by the Lady of the Lake; Tryfan above is claimed as his resting place.
s: The lake where legend says Excalibur was thrown
_facts: Ribbon lake between Carneddau and Glyderau
Legendary site of Excalibur's return to the Lady of the Lake
